grounds.point: Lakshmi Commercial Bank was the original tenant and was subsequently amalgamated with Canara Bank.
grounds.explanation: Both sides proceed on the basis that the premises had been let to Lakshmi Commercial Bank and that it was amalgamated with Canara Bank under the 1985 banking scheme. Section 14(1)(b) therefore requires assessment of whether the resulting change in possession or tenancy amounted to subletting, assignment or other parting with possession.

grounds.point: Canara Bank obtained and thereafter exercised exclusive possession of the premises as the successor occupant.
grounds.explanation: The landlord alleges that Lakshmi ceased to exist and possession passed to Canara, while Canara itself pleads exclusive possession since the amalgamation and argues that the lease and other assets and liabilities were taken over. General Radio treated analogous cessation of the transferor and succession to tenancy and possession as a transfer, and its account of Parasaram states that Delhi section 14(b) extends broadly to assignment or other modes of parting with possession, even an involuntary sale; General Radio itself arose under a different rent statute.

grounds.point: The supplied record identifies no written landlord consent to the succession, while Canara relies on implied consent and acquiescence.
grounds.explanation: Canara relies on the landlord's knowledge, acceptance of rent and long silence as implied consent or acquiescence; no written consent is identified in the supplied record. The quoted section 14(1)(b) expressly makes written landlord consent the relevant exception to otherwise qualifying subletting, assignment or parting with possession.

grounds.point: Court- or statute-mediated vesting does not, on the supplied authorities alone, establish an exemption from Delhi section 14(1)(b).
grounds.explanation: General Radio rejected the proposition that a company-initiated, court-sanctioned amalgamation was necessarily an involuntary transfer exempt from tenancy restrictions, and its discussion of Parasaram describes Delhi section 14(b) as broad. Telesound expressed a prima facie contrary view concerning statutory vesting but expressly reserved whether such amalgamation nevertheless amounted to an assignment attracting section 14(1)(b), leaving that issue for the rent authority.

grounds.point: A special statutory succession can preserve tenancy protection when the governing legislation expressly supplies that consequence.
grounds.explanation: Hindustan Petroleum upheld the successor's protection because the supplied acquisition legislation expressly vested the undertaking, made the Government the lessee or tenant, provided for renewal, and was followed by further statutory vesting. That authority therefore supports Canara only if the Banking Regulation Act scheme applicable here supplied a materially comparable tenancy-preserving consequence.

grounds.point: The supplied materials do not determine whether the Banking Regulation Act scheme expressly preserved or recreated the tenancy in Canara Bank so as to alter section 14(1)(b)'s ordinary transfer consequences.
grounds.explanation: The record shows that Canara produced the 23 August 1985 notification and asserts statutory amalgamation and takeover of the lease, but the supplied materials do not provide the operative Banking Regulation Act or scheme provisions defining the tenancy consequence. The authorities demonstrate materially different possibilities—transfer subject to rent restrictions in General Radio and expressly preserved tenancy protection in Hindustan Petroleum—so the legal effect of this particular statutory succession cannot be resolved from the supplied source version.

reason: The established succession, exclusive successor possession and absence of any identified written consent would support section 14(1)(b) if the 1985 banking amalgamation merely transferred Lakshmi's tenancy and possession to Canara. The ground remains UNDETERMINED because the supplied materials do not establish whether the governing Banking Regulation Act scheme instead expressly continued or created tenancy rights in the successor with a legal effect comparable to the special statutory protection recognized in Hindustan Petroleum.
